strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical perspective on multilingual visual supervision: captions originally produced in different languages may contribute complementary information. This is relevant to dataset construction, caption evaluation, and training data selection.

Comparing equal-sized caption sets for the same images is a sensible design for separating multilingual variation from ordinary caption variability. Table 1 reports substantial differences, including 3.71 objects for English–French–Chinese sets versus 2.59 for English-only sets.

Several complementary checks strengthen the descriptive finding. Visual Genome object coverage increases from 9.6% to 11.7% for Vertex in Table 3; the independent study with 20 participants and 30 images also reports increased multilingual coverage. Human translation evaluation provides reassuring evidence of semantic preservation.

The fine-tuning experiment holds training images constant and translates captions into English, reducing output-language compatibility as an explanation. In Table 15, matching-source models achieve the highest scores on six of seven language-specific test sets, supporting meaningful differences between caption distributions.
weaknesses: Result inconsistencies materially weaken confidence in this empirical contribution. All 36 entries in the LLaVA fine-tuning matrix in Table 14 exactly match the corresponding Vertex entries in Table 4, leaving the claimed independent replication unclear. Table 2 reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, although the seven entries average approximately 1.69. Table 15 also contradicts the claim that multilingual training ranks second on five languages: it ranks second on four, first on Chinese, and third on English and German. These affect quantitative conclusions and require reconciliation.

The expressive measurements are insufficiently validated. The translation study assesses conceptual fidelity, not preservation of LIWC tone, authenticity, or other psychological dimensions in short captions; its described sample also excludes human XM captions. Near-chance source-language prediction using a linear classifier on sentence embeddings does not establish that translation artifacts cannot affect these measurements. Table 7 explicitly includes spatial-relation and attribute corrections, so the assertion that translation corrections do not affect the measured content is too strong.

Section 3.2 does not support its proposed exclusion of language-specific model modes. Similar diversity between multilingual outputs and outputs from different English-captioning models places no established bound on the diversity that language-dependent decoding could produce. More generally, shared annotation instructions do not separate language from annotator population or culture. The results establish language-associated caption differences more convincingly than the suggested perceptual explanation.

Greater coverage is only partially connected to better visual supervision. There is no length-controlled analysis or systematic evaluation of the correctness of additional relations and attributes. Visual Genome object recall confirms some useful additions, but does not measure hallucination rates. Likewise, the fine-tuning results demonstrate adaptation to reference-caption distributions rather than improved visual understanding or robustness; multilingual training does not outperform French-only training on the mixed XM test set (0.151 versus 0.154).

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. Exact model checkpoints, generation settings, concept-merging thresholds, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and sufficiently detailed caption-sampling procedures are missing. The central tables lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability, despite claims of significant improvements. Together with the result inconsistencies and measurement limitations, these concerns outweigh the worthwhile descriptive findings and determine my Weak Reject recommendation.
